segments.text: 13 ships against 133 — an undefeated legend. Behind his resolve lay a two-thousand-year-old treatise on war.
Yi Sun-sin, Supreme Naval Commander of Joseon. He did not merely read the old texts — he rewrote them for the seas of Joseon.
Know yourself and know your enemy, and in a hundred battles you will win a hundred victories. Know yourself but not your enemy, and you will win one and lose one.

The original line in The Art of War reads 'in a hundred battles you will never be in peril.' But Yi Sun-sin rewrote it in his war diary as 'a hundred victories.' On a sea where a single defeat meant the end, merely avoiding peril was not enough. He had to win — and so he redrafted an ancient sentence into a doctrine of his own.

narrator.serviceGreeting: Welcome to the Feelandnote Library Tour, where we open the personal libraries of remarkable figures and explore the works they loved, and why.
narrator.celebIntro: Yi Sun-sin. A military commander of the Joseon dynasty who achieved the legendary record of 23 victories in 23 battles during the Japanese invasions of Korea. With his turtle ships and crane wing formation, he severed Japan's maritime supply lines, and at Myeongnyang he shattered 133 enemy ships with just 13 of his own, a miracle in naval history.
narrator.bridge: Now, let us open his library.
narrator.outro: Those were the five books that accompanied Admiral Yi Sun-sin through his campaigns. Curious about the deeper story of the commander who wielded a sword in one hand and a brush in the other? Discover more on Feel & Note.

host.bio: A military commander of the Joseon dynasty. A legendary admiral who defended his nation with extraordinary strategy and leadership during the Japanese invasions of Korea.
host.title: Admiral
host.featuredQuote: Move not rashly. Be still and resolute as a mountain.
host.philosophy: With my sword, I aimed at the enemy. With my brush, I steadied my soul. I made the wisdom of old war manuals my sail, the tears of my people my anchor. When the sea ran red with the blood of the fallen, I rewrote tomorrow for the living in black ink. Upon a pitch-black sea with nowhere to hide, these words that bound me fast were my only fortress.

books.title: The Art of War
books.creator: Sun Tzu
books.summary: A treatise on warfare written by Sun Tzu in the 5th century BC. The core of this book is one idea: win before you fight. 'First create the conditions for victory, then seek battle.' Deception, terrain, intelligence, the interplay of orthodox and unorthodox tactics — every strategy across its thirteen chapters exists to serve that single principle.
books.context: Yi Sun-sin passed the military examination in 1576. The Art of War was a required text, and he never set it aside after the exam. On November 28 of the Gabo year in his war diary, he copied a passage from Sun Tzu in his own hand. But there was one difference from the original. Where Sun Tzu wrote 'in a hundred battles you will never be in peril,' Yi Sun-sin changed it to 'in a hundred battles you will win a hundred victories.'
books.directQuote: Know yourself and know your enemy, and in a hundred battles you will win a hundred victories. Know yourself but not your enemy, and you will win one and lose one.
books.contextAfter: Merely avoiding peril was not enough for him. He built the conditions for certain victory himself. At Okpo, he commanded his men to be still as a mountain. At Hansan, he feigned retreat to lure the enemy into open waters. At Myeongnyang, he chose the narrow strait as his battlefield. For him, The Art of War was not a book to read — it was a book to write.

books.title: Wuzi
books.creator: Wu Qi
books.summary: A treatise on warfare written by the Warring States strategist Wu Qi in the 4th century BC. Where The Art of War addresses the principles of strategy, this book addresses the hearts of soldiers. Its central thesis: when a commander shares hardship and joy with his troops, those soldiers will not retreat even in the face of death. Wu Qi organized governance, command, and training into six chapters, and above all expounded the paradox that an army resolved to die will survive, while one desperate to live will perish.
books.context: Before the Battle of Myeongnyang, Yi Sun-sin drew a passage from this book. The original reads: 'He who is resolved to die shall live; he who hopes by chance to live shall die.' But he did not use the original words. Facing 133 ships with only 13, what was needed was an oath without a shred of doubt.
books.directQuote: He who is willing to die shall surely live. He who clings to life shall surely die.
books.contextAfter: He proved that oath first from his own ship. Standing alone at the front, he held for two hours, and thirteen ships destroyed thirty-one.

books.title: Romance of the Three Kingdoms
books.creator: Luo Guanzhong
books.summary: A historical novel written by Luo Guanzhong in the 14th century. Set against the backdrop of the Three Kingdoms era following the fall of the Han dynasty, it traces the saga from the Oath of the Peach Garden sworn by Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei to the rise and fall of three rival states. The story of Zhuge Liang is the novel's essence — devising the fire attack at the Red Cliffs, repelling an army by playing his lute in an empty fortress, and inscribing his loyalty in a single memorial to the throne. His narrative left a profound resonance across all of East Asia.
books.context: At the end of the Gabo year entries in his war diary, Yi Sun-sin copied a passage from Romance of the Three Kingdoms in his own hand.
books.directQuote: Outside, there is no one to set the nation right. Inside, there is no one to devise a plan.
books.contextAfter: For a man defending the sea alone amid the court's factional strife and incompetence, Zhuge Liang's lament could not have felt like someone else's story.

books.title: Classic of Poetry
books.creator: Unknown
books.summary: The earliest anthology of Chinese poetry, compiled between the 11th and 6th centuries BC. Tradition holds that Confucius selected 305 poems from over three thousand. From the songs of farmers tilling their fields to the ceremonial hymns of the royal court, no scene of human life is absent from this book. The Classic of Poetry stands as both a Confucian canon and an essential part of the East Asian literary tradition — the wellspring of a poetics that channels emotion into disciplined form.
books.context: In his war diary, Yi Sun-sin quoted the line 'Mother, O Heaven' from the Classic of Poetry. A commander longing for his mother on the battlefield reached for a line of verse written two thousand years before his time. Even a warrior at the front had feelings too deep for his own words. Throughout the war diary, traces of borrowed verse appear again and again. But on nights when the sound of a distant flute seeped through the dark, when borrowed words could not contain the weight of what he felt, he would take up the brush and write his own.
books.directQuote: Moonlit night on Hansan Isle, alone in the watchtower I sit. Great sword at my side, lost in deepening cares, when a lone flute pierces the dark, rending my very soul.
books.directQuoteSource: Nanjung Ilgi, Song of Hansan Isle
books.contextAfter: With words borrowed from the Classic of Poetry he called out to his mother, and atop the watchtower at Hansan he sang the night in words of his own.

books.title: New Tales Told by Lamplight
books.creator: Qu You
books.summary: A collection of fantastical tales written by Qu You of the Ming dynasty in 1378. Beneath the surface of ghosts and immortals lies a sharp satire of social corruption. The tale Yinghu Sheng Mingmeng Lu skewers a world where money can summon even the dead. This work traveled to Joseon and directly inspired Kim Si-seup's New Tales of the Golden Turtle.
books.context: In the Jeongyu year entries of his war diary, written in 1597, Yi Sun-sin quoted a line from this book. The local chief of Gwacheon, An Hong-je, had been arrested without cause and released only after surrendering a horse and servants as bribes. While men risked their lives at the front, this was what was happening behind the lines. Upon hearing the news, he wrote a bitter lament.
books.directQuote: So this is what they mean — a hundred coins can buy even a dead man's soul.
books.contextAfter: The world Qu You had satirized in fiction remained unchanged two hundred years later. In the war diary of a commander fighting for his life at sea, that satire was being recorded as fact.
